title: The other cheek (Matthew 5:38–42)
hook: no revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, go the second mile

segments.voice: Yesterday, let your yes be yes, and your line was yes means yes. Did you drop the boosters and just say what you meant? Day two hundred forty-six.

Somebody shoves you in line. Somebody posts something cruel about you. Somebody takes your parking space, then smirks. Everything in you wants to even the score. And maybe a little more than even, just so they learn. The next lines of the sermon are hard ones. Turn the other cheek. Go the extra mile. People who've never opened a Bible use them. But to hear them properly, you have to start with the old rule he's quoting.
screen: `EVEN THE SCORE.` → `TURN THE OTHER CHEEK.` → `START WITH THE OLD RULE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth." That's from the law of Moses. It's often read as a limit on revenge rather than a command to take it: one eye for one eye, not a whole family for an eye. And in Jewish tradition, the rabbis read it as fair compensation paid in court, not literal injury. Jesus goes further still. "But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." Then three pictures. If someone sues you for your coat, give him your cloak too. And, in the King James Bible: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." That word compel had a specific use: scholars say it meant soldiers and officials pressing locals into service, like carrying gear. It's the same Greek word Mark uses when the soldiers compel Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross. So picture it: a soldier of the occupying army orders you to haul his pack. The order is one mile. Jesus says: go two. Scholars read these sayings in different ways. Some, like the scholar Walter Wink, argue that a slap on the right cheek was a backhanded insult, and turning the other cheek was a nonviolent way of standing your ground with dignity. Others read it more simply as refusing to retaliate at all. Churches differ, too: the peace churches say it rules out violence entirely; many other Christians say it governs personal revenge, not every use of force. What these readings share is the direction: break the cycle. Don't pay back.
screen: `AN EYE FOR AN EYE: A LIMIT.` · `TURN TO HIM THE OTHER ALSO.` · `COMPEL: A SOLDIER'S PACK.` · `BREAK THE CYCLE.` · then, large: `GO WITH HIM TWAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go one extra mile for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who asks more of you than you'd like: a demanding boss, a needy relative, a neighbor who always wants a favor. Picture the thing they usually ask for. Now picture doing that, and then a little more, freely, before they ask. Not because you have to. Because you choose to. If it would put you in danger or let someone abuse you, that's not this. If you pray, you can ask for a free heart. The bell holds the time.
The other cheek. No revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, and when you're forced to go one mile, go two.
Your line: the second mile. Today, when someone asks something of you, do what they asked, and then one small thing more, freely. Day two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: The peace churches, such as Mennonites, Quakers and the Church of the Brethren, read this as a call to nonviolence; many other Christians apply it to personal insult and revenge, and practice it through forgiveness and generosity.

fork.setup: a Roman soldier orders you to carry his pack for a mile. you reach the milestone. what does Jesus say to do?
fork.reveal: "whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain." do more than you're forced to, freely.

original.note: Greek: shall compel, press into service. Matthew 5:41; Mark 15:21 uses it of Simon of Cyrene.

trapdoor: what you thought: turn the other cheek means be a doormat.
what it means: refuse to pay back; break the cycle of revenge, and do more good than is demanded.
